You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'Dual-Ended-Boost': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 3aa2497495a1).
L1 L pzp n1 0.001
S1 S n1 0 ctrl=G1
D1 D n1 out DSCH
G1 SYNC ton=0.0001s phase=0 edges=pos

screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: 0.567 uW of 0.476 uW needed (119 %); S4: -1.47 uW of 0.147 uW needed (-999 %); S6: -2.9 uW of 0.324 uW needed (-894 %)
what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -999 % of the load's need on S4 (weakest excitation), -894 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   `vavg` >= 1.8 V (S1-S6)
        *   `vmax` <= 3.6 V (S1-S6)
        *   `vpp` <= 0.05 V (S1-S6)
        *   `tup` <= 0.4 s (cold start)
        *   `dv` <= 0.02 V (settled)
    *   Piezo Model: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $R_{\text{leak}} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$ (S1), $I_p = 12\text{ }\mu\text{A}$ (S1).
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude $V_{\text{oc}} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 0.76\text{ V}$.
    *   Crucial Observation: $V_{\text{oc}}$ (0.76 V) is significantly lower than the required $V_{\text{out}}$ (1.8 V). This means a simple bridge rectifier (FBR) cannot work (it only delivers $V_{\text{oc}} - 2V_{\text{diode}}$). A voltage-boosting mechanism (like SSHI or Boost converter) is *essential*.

    *   `P-SSHI` (Parallel Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):
        *   Screen results: High power (2384%-4542%).
        *   Sim results: `vavg` near 0 V.
        *   Analysis: The screen (out fixed at 1.8 V) works, but the actual simulation fails. Looking at the connectivity: `D1: pzp -> out`, `D2: pzn -> out`, `D3: 0 -> pzp`, `D4: 0 -> pzn`.
        *   Wait, `D3` and `D4` are diodes from 0 to pzp/pzn. This looks like a full bridge, but with anodes at ground?
        *   Correct Full Bridge: `D1: pzp -> out`, `D2: pzn -> out`, `D3: 0 -> pzp`, `D4: 0 -> pzn`? No, if `D3` is `0 -> pzp`, current flows from 0 to pzp. This is wrong.
        *   Correct Bridge: `D1: pzp -> out`, `D2: pzn -> out`, `D3: 0 -> pzp` (NO), `D3: pzp -> 0` (NO), `D3: 0 -> pzp` is wrong.
        *   Let's re-read the reference: `full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        *   Wait, the reference says `["0", "pzp"]` is a return diode. That means anode is 0, cathode is pzp. Let's check the flow.
        *   When `pzp` is negative, current flows from `pzp` to `0`? No, if diode is `0 -> pzp`, current flows `0` to `pzp`.
        *   Let's re-evaluate the Bridge Rectifier:
            - Path 1: `pzp` (+) -> `D1` -> `out` -> `RL` -> `0` -> `D4` -> `pzn` (-).
            - Path 2: `pzn` (+) -> `D2` -> `out` -> `RL` -> `0` -> `D3` -> `pzp` (-).
            - So the diodes are: `[pzp, out]`, `[pzn, out]`, `[0, pzp]`, `[0, pzn]`.
        *   Wait, `P-SSHI` used: `D1: pzp out`, `D2: pzn out`, `D3: 0 pzp`, `D4: 0 pzn`. This *is* a bridge.
        *   Why did `P-SSHI` fail in simulation? `L1: pzp n1`, `S1: n1 pzn`.
        *   This is an SSHI-like flipping circuit. SSHI usually flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
        *   In the `P-SSHI` design: `S1` connects `pzp` (via `L1`) to `pzn`. This flips the charge on $C_p$.
        *   But the diodes `D1-D4` are in parallel with the piezo.
        *   If $V_{\text{out}}$ is 1.8 V, and $V_{\text{oc}}$ is 0.76 V, the diodes `D1` and `D2` will never conduct unless the flipping increases the voltage across $C_p$ significantly.
        *   SSHI goal: Increase voltage across $C_p$ to $V_{\text{out}} + V_{\text{diode}}$.
        *   The `P-SSHI` structure seems correct in theory, but maybe the switching timing or the interaction with the bridge is wrong. The screen says it *can* deliver power if `out` is fixed, but the real simulation doesn't start.

    *   `Dual-Ended-Boost`: failed screen (S4: -999%). This was an attempt at a boost converter.

    *   The key problem is "Cold Start". We need to get from 0 V to 1.8 V.
    *   A simple bridge (FBR) fails because $V_{\text{oc}} < 1.8 \text{ V} + 2 V_{\text{diode}}$.
    *   SSHI is the standard way to solve this for piezo.
    *   Standard SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):
        - A switch and an inductor are used to invert the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks of the displacement (which correspond to the extrema of the voltage).
        - This avoids the "dead zone" where the piezo voltage is lower than the storage capacitor voltage.
    *   Let's refine the SSHI topology.
    *   The structure of `P-SSHI` provided was:
        `D1: pzp out`, `D2: pzn out`, `D3: 0 pzp`, `D4: 0 pzn` (Full Bridge)
        `L1: pzp n1`, `S1: n1 pzn` (Flip circuit)
        `G1: SYNC ton=... phase=... edges=both`
    *   Wait, if the bridge is `D1-D4`, the flip circuit `S1` should be across the piezo.
    *   When $V_{\text{pzp}} - V_{\text{pzn}}$ reaches a peak, we close `S1` to flip the voltage.
    *   Is `S1` connected correctly? `L1` from `pzp` to `n1`, `S1` from `n1` to `pzn`. This creates a loop: `pzp -> L1 -> n1 -> S1 -> pzn -> C_p -> pzp`. This is correct.
    *   Why did it fail? Maybe the bridge diodes are too restrictive or the `S1` flip is interfering with the bridge?
    *   Actually, look at the `P-SSHI` simulation results: `vavg` is nearly 0. The screen worked (fixed `out` = 1.8 V), but the real simulation didn't. This suggests it can *maintain* 1.8 V but cannot *reach* it (cold start).
    *   Wait, the screen says "out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers...". If it delivers power at 1.8 V, it *should* be able to charge a capacitor to 1.8 V.
    *   Why did the simulation fail then? `vmax` was 0.216 V. This is very strange. If it can deliver power at 1.8 V, it should charge the capacitor.
    *   Let's re-read: "vavg -0.0296 V... V(out) never exceeds 0.22 V". This means the `P-SSHI` structure is not actually working in the simulation.
    *   Wait! Look at the `P-SSHI` components again: `D3: 0 pzp`, `D4: 0 pzn`.
    *   If $V_{\text{pzp}}$ is negative, `D3` (0 to pzp) conducts. $V_{\text{pzp}}$ is clamped to $-0.25\text{ V}$.
    *   If $V_{\text{pzn}}$ is negative, `D4` (0 to pzn) conducts. $V_{\text{pzn}}$ is clamped to $-0.25\text{ V}$.
    *   This is a standard bridge.
    *   Maybe the `S1` switch timing is the problem? `phase=0.17`, `edges=both`.
    *   In a piezo, the voltage peaks when the current is zero. The SYNC controller closes at "piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current".
    *   So `phase=0` is exactly at the peak.
    *   If `P-SSHI` failed the simulation but passed the screen, there's a contradiction. Let me re-read the screen: "S2: 11.3 uW of 0.476 uW needed (2364 %)". This is huge.
    *   Why would it fail in sim? Ah, maybe the `L1` value is too high or `ton` is too long, causing the voltage to flip *too much* or causing a short? No, the screen also uses those values.
    *   Let's try a different approach: **SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction)**.
    *   SECE is often more robust than SSHI.
    *   Basic SECE:
        - An inductor `L` and a switch `S` are used to extract charge at the peaks.
        - Circuit: `L` from `pzp` to `n1`, `S` from `n1` to `out`, `D` from `out` to `n1`.
        - Or simpler: `S` connects `pzp` to `L`, `L` to `out` (via a diode).
    *   Let's try a simple **Inductive Boost** (or "Dickson-like" but with an inductor).
    *   Actually, the most reliable piezo circuit for low $V_{\text{oc}}$ is a **Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI)** but with a different configuration.
    *   Wait, I have an idea. Let's try a **Half-Bridge SSHI** (only one side).
    *   Or better, a **Standard Boost Converter** approach.
    *   Let's look at the "Dual-Ended-Boost" that failed the screen.
        `L1 L pzp n1`, `S1 S n1 0 ctrl=G1`, `D1 D n1 out`, `G1 SYNC edges=pos`.
        `L2 L pzn n2`, `S2 S n2 0 ctrl=G2`, `D2 D n2 out`, `G2 SYNC edges=neg`.
        This is a boost converter. Why did it fail the screen?
        `S4: -1.47 uW of 0.147 uW needed`.
        A negative power means it's consuming power from the output.
        The `S1` switch connects `n1` to `0`. This means `L1` charges from `pzp`.
        When `S1` opens, `L1` discharges through `D1` to `out`.
        Wait, if `S1` connects `n1` to `0`, the loop is `pzp -> L1 -> n1 -> S1 -> 0`.
        But `pzp` is a current source.
        The energy is stored in $C_p$.
        When `S1` is closed, the voltage $V_{\text{pzp}}$ is clamped to 0. The current $I_p$ charges $L_1$.
        This doesn't seem right. The energy in $C_p$ should be transferred to $L_1$.
        For that, `S1` should connect `pzp` and `L1` to `0` *at the peak* of $V_{\text{pzp}}$.
        Correct Boost:
        1. Piezo charges $C_p$ (open circuit).
        2. At $V_{\text{peak}}$, close `S1` to connect $C_p$ to $L_1$ and ground.
        3. $C_p$ discharges into $L_1$.
        4. Open `S1`, $L_1$ pushes charge through `D1` to `out`.

    *   Let's refine this:
        `L1` from `pzp` to `n1`.
        `S1` from `n1` to `0`.
        `D1` from `n1` to `out`.
        Wait, this is exactly what "Dual-Ended-Boost" did. Why did it fail the screen?
        Maybe because `pzp` is a current source, not a voltage source?
        In the piezo model, the current source $I_p$ is in parallel with $C_p$.
        So the total current is $I_p + C_p(dv/dt)$.
        If we close `S1`, we are shorting $C_p$ through $L_1$ to ground. This is exactly how you extract energy from $C_p$.
        Why was the power negative?
        Maybe `S1` is closed too long or at the wrong time?
        The screen tests "best of the value presets". If the values were $L=1\text{ mH}$, $t_{\text{on}}=100\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, it should work.
        Let's look at the `S4` failure again: `-1.47 uW`. This means the circuit is leaking.
        Where is the leak? `D1` is `n1` to `out`. `D2` is `n2` to `out`.
        Is there a path from `out` to `0`?
        `S1` is `n1` to `0`. If `S1` is closed, and `D1` is `n1` to `out`, then `out` is connected to `0` through `D1` and `S1`.
        YES! That's the leak.
        When `S1` is closed, `out` is connected to ground via `D1` (which is reverse biased? No, `D1` is `n1` to `out`. If `S1` is closed, `n1` is 0. `D1` is `0` to `out`. This is reverse biased. No leak there).
        Wait, `D1` is `n1` to `out`. `S1` is `n1` to `0`.
        `out` -> `D1` (cathode) -> `n1` (anode) -> `S1` -> `0`.
        This is a reverse-biased diode. It shouldn't leak.
        Wait, I see the problem. `S1` is `n1` to `0`. `D1` is `n1` to `out`.
        If `S1` is closed, $V_{\text{n1}} = 0$. `D1` has anode at 0 and cathode at $V_{\text{out}}$. This is reverse-biased.
        So where is the leak?
        Let's check the other side: `L2` from `pzn` to `n2`, `S2` from `n2` to `0`, `D2` from `n2` to `out`.
        Same thing.
        Wait, what about the `Dret1` and `Dret2` in the "Dual-Ended-Boost"?
        `Dret1: 0 pzn`, `Dret2: 0 pzp`.
        These are diodes from ground to the piezo.
        If $V_{\text{pzn}}$ is negative, `Dret1` (0 to pzn) conducts.
        This is just a half-bridge.
        Maybe the "Dual-Ended-Boost" failed because it was too complex?

    *   Let's try a simpler, more proven topology: **The SSHI with a single-ended rectifier**.
        Actually, a **Full-Bridge Rectifier** with an **Inductive Flip** is a very strong candidate.
        Wait, I already tried `P-SSHI` and it failed. Let me look at its `D3` and `D4` again.
        `D3: 0 pzp`, `D4: 0 pzn`.
        These are the return diodes of the bridge.
        If `pzp` is negative, `D3` (0 to pzp) conducts.
        This is correct.
        Wait, I just realized why `P-SSHI` failed in simulation but passed the screen.
        The screen fixes `out` at 1.8 V.
        The simulation starts at `out` = 0 V.
        In `P-SSHI`, the flipping is done by `S1` and `L1`.
        If `out` is 0, the bridge diodes `D1` and `D2` will conduct as soon as $|V_{\text{pzp}}| > 0.25\text{ V}$.
        This will charge `out` to $0.76\text{ V} - 0.25\text{ V} = 0.51\text{ V}$.
        But to reach 1.8 V, we need the flipping to work.
        The flip circuit `S1` connects `pzp` and `pzn` through `L1`.
        This flips the voltage across $C_p$.
        If $V_{\text{pzp}}$ was $0.5\text{ V}$, after flip it becomes $-0.5\text{ V}$.
        The total voltage difference is $1.0\text{ V}$.
        This can help charge the capacitor higher.
        However, if the flip happens *while* the diodes are conducting, the energy is just dumped.
        The flip must happen *at the peak* of the voltage, when the diodes are just about to stop conducting.

    *   Let's try a **Buck-Boost** like structure that is known to work for piezo:
        1.  Piezo $C_p$ is charged.
        2.  A switch `S` connects $C_p$ to an inductor `L` and a diode `D` to `out`.
        3.  This is effectively a boost converter.
